analysis.one_liner: Restricts IRS audit and enforcement funding and blocks donor-disclosure rules for tax-exempt political groups.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate Finance Committee hearing or a vote; it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would freeze IRS audit and enforcement funding at 2021 levels until the agency published an updated projection of the tax gap — the difference between taxes owed and taxes collected — and would bar new enforcement targeting households earning under $400,000. It would also exempt most tax-exempt organizations, including politically active 501(c) groups, from naming their donors on IRS filings, raise penalties for leaking taxpayer information, and create an IRS fellowship program to recruit outside tax experts for complex audits. The stated aim was to limit what supporters saw as IRS overreach; critics said it would make it easier for high earners and large organizations to avoid taxes already owed. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy taxpayers and large organizations that might face more aggressive IRS audits benefit from the funding freeze and enforcement caps. Tax-exempt political organizations benefit from being able to accept large contributions without naming their donors to the IRS. Taxpayers who fear IRS overreach or data leaks benefit from the higher penalties for unauthorized disclosure and the ban on auditing households under $400,000. The IRS itself would gain the fellowship program and AI tools, though only within the funding limits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and tax-exempt political groups

how_it_helps.text: Forbids the IRS from spending any enforcement money above fiscal 2021 levels until 180 days after it publishes an updated tax-gap projection, and sunsets that restriction after one year.
Bars new funding for auditing taxpayers with incomes under $400,000 and for IRS bank-account reporting requirements, and blocks new National Research Program audit expansion beyond 2021 levels.
Exempts most tax-exempt organizations from naming their donors on IRS filings, and lets most 501(c) groups stop reporting contributor names and addresses.
Raises the penalty for IRS employees or tax preparers who leak taxpayer information from $5,000 to $250,000, and eases procedures for firing employees who commit such disclosures.
Prohibits IRS employees from using official union time during tax filing season (February 12 to April 15).

Creates a fellowship program to recruit private-sector tax experts into an IRS audit task force, and directs the IRS to use artificial intelligence to estimate the tax gap and target enforcement at nonfilers and complex corporate returns.

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, compliant taxpayers would pay more over time: weaker enforcement means the taxes others legally owe go uncollected, shifting the burden to people who pay. The public also loses information about who funds tax-exempt political organizations when donor names come off the filings.

drawbacks.text: The bill freezes IRS audit and enforcement funding at fiscal year 2021 levels for up to a year, which the IRS and outside analysts say would slow collection of taxes already owed — money that would otherwise reduce deficits or fund other priorities.
By barring contributor names and addresses from nonprofit returns, the bill makes it harder for the public to trace large donations flowing through tax-exempt groups into political activity.

The bill caps National Research Program audits at fiscal 2021 levels and mandates new data requirements before enforcement expansion, which an honest supporter would acknowledge delays and complicates tax collection even while citing fraud-reduction goals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles some genuinely appealing ideas — hiring experienced tax experts, tougher penalties for leaking taxpayer data, limits on auditing households under $400,000 — but its central mechanism ties the agency's hands: enforcement funding stays frozen until the IRS produces an annual tax-gap projection the law itself defines tightly, and corporate audit selection is constrained. Weaker audits of the sophisticated returns where unpaid taxes concentrate, combined with exempting political nonprofits from naming their donors, shift real costs onto compliant taxpayers and voters. The one-year sunset on the funding freeze limits the damage, but on balance the bill's design favors limiting scrutiny of large, complex filers more than it favors taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2022, and the committee never took it up before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 7, 2022 by Senator Mike Braun with no cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
No cosponsors ever joined the bill.
No further action was recorded; the Congress ended January 3, 2023, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Groups opposing IRS enforcement — including wealthy taxpayers facing potential audits and donors to politically active tax-exempt groups — are better off because the bill never had to be defeated; it simply lapsed. Had it passed, compliant taxpayers would have indirectly borne the cost of a weaker enforcement posture.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of IRS enforcement, since the bill died quietly

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and read it twice on the Senate floor, sending it to the Finance Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so the measure never drew enough recorded support or opposition to show a partisan pattern.

industries.note: Frozen enforcement funding and capped audit expansion mean less capacity to pursue unpaid taxes at the top of the income distribution. The bill's own data-projection requirement delays any enforcement increase.
The bill lets most 501(c) organizations and many other tax-exempt groups file returns without naming their contributors, shielding the money trail behind political activity.

industries.industry: Tax preparers and data firms handling taxpayer data
industries.note: The bill raises the penalty for unauthorized disclosure of taxpayer information from $1,000 to $250,000, raising the cost of leaks and misuse of client data.

industries.industry: IRS workforce and federal employee unions
industries.note: Union official time is banned during filing season and employees who leak taxpayer data face easier removal, while a new fellowship program would hire outside tax experts at GS-15-level pay to handle complex audits.
